title: A producer-consumer pipeline on virtual threads

blocks.text: The page's point about compatibility: `java.util.concurrent` works unchanged on virtual threads. A `BlockingQueue` producer-consumer pipeline is written exactly as before; a virtual thread waiting in `take()` just unmounts instead of holding an OS thread.
Write `Pipeline.run(List<String> items, Function<String, String> stage, int workers)`:

items: One **producer** virtual thread puts every item on a `BlockingQueue`.
`workers` **worker** virtual threads, running at the same time, take items from the queue and pass each through `stage`.
When the items run out, **every** worker stops (a common way: the producer puts one "poison pill" per worker after the items; compare it by identity).
Workers add their results from several threads, so collect them thread-safely (the tests cannot force two adds to collide, so that part is not graded).
`run` returns all the stage results (in any order) only once the producer and all workers have finished, however long a stage call takes.

rows: each call waits until 3 calls are in progress

cases.says: run passes every item through the stage exactly once and returns all the results.
With 3 workers, three stage calls that each wait for the other two all finish: the workers really run at once.
run returns once the items are done: every worker is told to stop, not just one.
run does not return while a stage call is still in progress, however long it takes.
An item equal to "" is processed like any other: the end marker is recognised by identity, not by equals.
Once run returns, every worker thread has ended: none is left blocked on the queue.
Every stage call runs on a virtual thread.

concepts: java.util.concurrent tools such as BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch and ExecutorService work unchanged on virtual threads, and a virtual thread waiting in take() unmounts.
